html:
The 1997 Southeast Asian haze was a cloud of smoke that covered much of Southeast Asia for months in the second half of 1997. It came from fires in Indonesia, above all on Sumatra and in Kalimantan on Borneo.

Fire had long been used to clear land, but by the 1990s companies and smallholders were burning huge areas of forest and drained peat swamp for oil palm and pulpwood. In 1997 a strong El Niño brought drought, the rains came late, and the fires ran out of control. Burning peat smoulders for weeks and gives off thick smoke.

The haze spread over Malaysia, Singapore, Brunei and southern Thailand. Schools closed, flights were cancelled, and many thousands of people sought treatment for breathing problems. In September 1997 a passenger plane crashed near Medan in poor visibility. Costs were later put at about 9 billion US dollars. The disaster hit just as the Asian financial crisis was striking the same countries.

Haze has returned in many dry years since. ASEAN signed an agreement on cross-border haze pollution in 2002, though fires still flare.
